body:
Socio-religious reform in colonial India

During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, different Indian communities began questioning established social practices and seeking changes in religious and everyday life. These efforts are called socio-religious reform movements because they addressed religious beliefs as well as social customs, education and community welfare.

Reform did not take the same form everywhere. Its character depended on the problems experienced by each community. Among the Parsis, educated reformers used associations, newspapers and schools to reconsider religious practices and promote education. Among several Adivasi communities, religious renewal was closely connected with the protection of land, resistance to exploitation and the assertion of community identity.

Parsi reform: religion, education and public debate

The Parsis are an Indian community whose religious tradition is Zoroastrianism, which originated in ancient Persia. Important Parsi settlements developed in western India, particularly in Gujarat and Bombay. Surat and Navsari were significant centres of Parsi community life.

In nineteenth-century Bombay, exposure to modern education, missionary criticism of Zoroastrian beliefs and discussion within the community encouraged reformers to examine inherited customs. Their principal methods included organised meetings, lectures, publications and educational institutions. Reformers generally sought to strengthen their religious tradition by distinguishing its essential teachings from practices they regarded as unnecessary additions.

Tribal reform: community renewal and social justice

The term Adivasi refers to communities commonly described as tribal or indigenous communities in India. These communities had different languages, beliefs, livelihoods and social arrangements. Therefore, there was no single tribal reform movement representing all Adivasis.

In several regions, religious leaders urged followers to abandon liquor, reject practices they considered harmful, improve cleanliness and build community unity. Such programmes could also challenge landlords, moneylenders, officials and other powerful groups. Where land and livelihood were threatened, religious reform sometimes developed into organised political resistance.

Why the distinction matters

Religious reform concerns beliefs, rituals and moral conduct. Social reform addresses practices such as unequal access to education or harmful customs. Political and agrarian resistance challenges authority, land dispossession or economic exploitation. A single movement may contain more than one of these elements.

The Parsi reform association established in Bombay in 1851, Birsa Munda's movement in Chotanagpur, the Bhil movement associated with Govind Guru and the Devi movement of South Gujarat illustrate different combinations of these aims.

Prelims focus

  • Parsi reform was particularly associated with Bombay and western India's educated public sphere.
  • Parsis follow the Zoroastrian religious tradition.
  • Tribal religious movements could combine moral reform with demands concerning land, labour and community autonomy.
  • Trap: A tribal movement involving religious beliefs was not necessarily limited to worship; it could also oppose economic and political exploitation.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts–III, chapters 'Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age' and 'Women, Caste and Reform', printed pp. 39–49 and 95–96; Dinyar Patel, 'Our Own Religion in Ancient Persia', Global Intellectual History, 2017, pp. 313–315.]

title: Parsi and Tribal Reform: Two Important Streams of Social Change

body:
Establishment of the reform association

The Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha, also written as Rahnumae Mazdayasnan Sabha, was established in Bombay in 1851. Its name broadly refers to a society guiding followers of the Mazdayasnan or Zoroastrian religious path. It became an important organisation for religious reform among Parsis.

The Sabha emerged when educated Parsis were responding to criticism of Zoroastrianism by Christian missionaries and discussing changes within their own community. Its reformers argued that the original Zoroastrian faith was rational and morally valuable, but that some customary practices had developed over time and should be reconsidered.

Important personalities

Naoroji Furdonji, also spelled Navrozji Fardunji, was the Sabha's first president. Dadabhai Naoroji served as its first secretary. Other notable reform-minded associates included Sorabjee Shapoorjee Bengalee and Kharshedji Rustamji Cama.

Naoroji Furdonji and Dadabhai Naoroji were different people. Naoroji Furdonji was the Sabha's first president, while Dadabhai Naoroji was its first secretary. Similar-sounding names should not be confused in matching questions.

Ideas and methods of reform

The Sabha did not seek to replace Zoroastrianism with another religion. It advocated returning to what reformers understood as the simpler and purer teachings of their ancestral faith. Its activities included lectures, discussion of religious texts, public meetings and publications.

Reformers questioned practices that they regarded as inconsistent with the central teachings of Zoroastrianism. They also supported wider social improvement, particularly the spread of education and discussion about the position of women. Their proposals encountered resistance from conservative members of the community, showing that Parsi society did not speak with a single voice on reform.

Rast Goftar and the role of Gujarati journalism

In 1851, Dadabhai Naoroji and fellow reformers helped launch Rast Goftar, meaning Truth Teller, a Gujarati-language newspaper. It became an influential means of discussing religious customs, women's education and social change.

Its importance lay in the use of print to carry arguments beyond individual meetings. Readers could encounter reformist ideas, evaluate criticism and participate in a larger public discussion. This also illustrates the place of the Gujarati language in the development of modern reformist journalism in western India.

Prelims focus

  • 1851: Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha established in Bombay.
  • Naoroji Furdonji: first president of the Sabha.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji: first secretary of the Sabha.
  • Rast Goftar: Gujarati-language reform newspaper launched in 1851.
  • Trap: Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha was an association; Rast Goftar was a newspaper.

[Sources: Dinyar Patel, 'Our Own Religion in Ancient Persia: Dadabhai Naoroji and Orientalist Scholarship on Zoroastrianism', Global Intellectual History, vol. 2, no. 3, 2017, pp. 313–315; J. N. Farquhar, Modern Religious Movements in India, chapter 'Movements Favouring Vigorous Reform', section on Parsi reform; University of Mumbai, History of Modern Maharashtra, section on Parsi social reform and Rast Goftar, printed p. 106.]

pictures.alt: The Sabha was a religious reform association; Rast Goftar was a Gujarati newspaper. Both supported religious discussion, social improvement and education.
pictures.caption: The Sabha and Rast Goftar served different but complementary purposes.

title: Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha and the Parsi Religious Reform Movement

body:
Education as an instrument of social reform

Nineteenth-century Parsi reformers regarded education as a means of improving individual opportunities and community life. Education could help people read religious works, examine inherited customs and participate in public discussion. Girls' education was especially significant because many families across colonial Indian society considered advanced schooling unnecessary or inappropriate for girls.

Among Parsis in Bombay, organised efforts to expand schooling for boys and girls were underway by 1849. These initiatives formed part of a larger movement that connected education with religious and social improvement.

Manockjee Cursetjee and girls' education

Manockjee Cursetjee was an important Parsi supporter of women's education. On 1 September 1863, he established the Alexandra Native Girls' English Institution in Bombay. The school initially operated from premises provided at his residence, Villa Byculla.

Although its founder was a Zoroastrian, the institution admitted girls from different castes and communities. Its aim therefore extended beyond education for Parsi girls alone. The institution later became known as the Alexandra Girls' English Institution.

A school founded by a Parsi reformer should not automatically be classified as a school exclusively for Parsis. The Alexandra Native Girls' English Institution was explicitly opened to girls from different communities.

Behramji Malabari and wider social reform

Behramji M. Malabari was a Parsi journalist and social reformer associated with the newspaper Indian Spectator. He campaigned against infant marriage and enforced widowhood, particularly practices that deprived young girls and widows of dignity and personal choice.

In 1884, Malabari circulated writings known as his Notes on Infant Marriage and Enforced Widowhood. They encouraged wider public discussion and government attention to the condition of women. His campaign addressed Indian society beyond the Parsi community.

The Age of Consent Act, 1891

The Age of Consent Act, 1891 raised the age of consent for girls from 10 to 12 years under the relevant criminal law of that period. This was one result of broader nineteenth-century debates over the protection of girls, to which Malabari contributed.

Age of consent and minimum age of marriage are different legal concepts. The 1891 change concerned the age below which sexual intercourse was treated as an offence under the applicable law; it did not establish 12 years as a general statutory minimum age for marriage. The later Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929 addressed the restraint of child marriages through a separate legislative measure.

The western Indian connection

The Parsi community's historical presence in Surat and Navsari, together with reformist activity in Bombay and the use of Gujarati newspapers, linked Parsi social reform to the wider history of western India. The location of the Alexandra institution, however, was Bombay, not Surat or Navsari.

Prelims focus

  • 1863: Manockjee Cursetjee founded the Alexandra Native Girls' English Institution in Bombay.
  • 1884: Behramji Malabari circulated writings against infant marriage and enforced widowhood.
  • 1891: The Age of Consent Act raised the relevant age of consent from 10 to 12 years.
  • 1929: The Child Marriage Restraint Act dealt separately with child marriage.
  • Trap: The Age of Consent Act, 1891, did not make 12 years the general legal minimum marriage age.

[Sources: J. N. Farquhar, Modern Religious Movements in India, chapter 'Movements Favouring Vigorous Reform', section on Parsi education; Alexandra Girls' English Institution, official institutional history, 'Foundation of AGEI' (consulted 20 November 2026); Supreme Court of India, Society for Enlightenment and Voluntary Action v. Union of India, judgment dated 18 October 2024, paragraphs 22–28; NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts–III, chapter 'Women, Caste and Reform', printed pp. 97–101.]

pictures.alt: Timeline from Parsi schooling in 1849 to the 1891 Age of Consent Act, distinguishing education, community reform, journalism and legislation.
pictures.caption: Educational initiatives, organised Parsi reform and wider social legislation developed over several decades.

title: Parsi Educational Initiatives, Women's Reform and Behramji Malabari

body:
Changes in land, forests and livelihoods

Many Adivasi communities depended on land, forests, cultivation, grazing and forest products. Colonial policies increasingly altered these relationships. Forest regulations restricted access to resources, while new arrangements of land ownership and revenue collection weakened customary rights in some regions.

Landlords, traders and moneylenders gained influence in areas where Adivasi households were vulnerable to debt. Some communities also faced demands for labour, including unpaid or compulsory work. These difficulties varied from region to region; they were not experienced identically by every tribal community.

Who were the dikus?

In accounts of the Munda movement, the term diku refers to outsiders regarded as exploiting or dominating tribal society. Depending on the local situation, these could include moneylenders, landlords, traders and other agents of outside authority.

The central grievance was not simply that such people came from outside a village. It was that their activities were associated with the loss of land, increasing debt, oppressive labour demands or interference with community life.

Why religion became a means of mobilisation

Religious and moral teachings were familiar ways of organising community life. A leader who spoke of purification, honesty, abstinence or the restoration of ancestral traditions could attract followers seeking both social improvement and relief from exploitation.

Religious messages helped establish shared rules of behaviour and collective identity. For example, a call to stop drinking alcohol could be presented as moral reform; in a region where liquor traders were also powerful creditors, the same action might reduce dependence on those traders.

Reform was not the same as rebellion

Different movements used different methods. Some emphasised prayer, changed customs and peaceful withdrawal from exploitative relationships. Others confronted authorities over land or political control. A movement could also change character over time.

The Santhal uprising of 1855 is a well-known example of tribal rebellion against exploitation and colonial authority. It should not be confused with later religious reform movements among the Mundas, Oraons and Bhils. The groups, leaders and immediate aims were not identical.

Prelims focus

  • Diku: a term used in the Munda context for outsiders regarded as exploiters.
  • Forest restrictions, land alienation, debt and labour demands were important sources of tribal discontent.
  • Tribal reform often sought changes in social conduct alongside resistance to exploitation.
  • 1855: the Santhal uprising was distinct from Birsa Munda's later movement.
  • Trap: Tribal reform, tribal rebellion and organised welfare work are related but different forms of activity.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts–III, chapter 'Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age', printed pp. 39–49; NCERT, Class 9, India and the Contemporary World–I, chapter 'Forest Society and Colonialism', section 'Why Deforestation?', printed pp. 78–80.]

pictures.alt: Shared colonial pressures could encourage religious renewal, community solidarity and organised resistance, without every movement becoming violent.
pictures.caption: Religious and social reform could arise from the same conditions that produced agrarian grievances.

title: The Background of Tribal Religious Reform under Colonial Rule
